'''Ame no Wakahiko''' (天稚彦 or 天若日子) is a god of grains and ''[[Amatsukami]]'' in [[Japanese mythology]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=天若日子{{!}}アメノワカヒコ{{!}}日本神話の世界|url=https://www.shinwanosekai.info/amenowakahiko.php|access-date=2020-09-29 |website=www.shinwanosekai.info}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=天若日子 京都通百科事典|url=https://www.kyototuu.jp/Jinjya/MikotoAmenowakahiko.html|access-date=2020-09-29|website=京都通百科事典|language=ja}}</ref> He is the son of [[Amatsukunitama]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto - Home: Kami in Classic Texts: Ame no Wakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|access-date=2020-09-29|website=eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp}}</ref> The ''{{ill|Ame no Wakahiko Monogatari|ja|天稚彦草子|qid=Q22125968}}'', one of the ''[[Otogi-zōshi]]'', is a ''{{ill|Monogatari|be|Манагатары|ca|Monogatari|de|Monogatari|es|Monogatari|eu|Monogatari|fa|مونوگاتاری (داستان)|fi|Monogatari|fr|Monogatari|hak|Vu̍t-ngî|hu|Monogatari|id|Monogatari|it|Monogatari|ja|物語 (日本文学)|ka|მონოგატარი|kk|Моногатари|ko|모노가타리|pl|Monogatari|pt|Monogatari|ru|Моногатари|tr|Monogatari|uk|Моноґатарі|vi|Monogatari|zh|物语|zh_min_nan|Bu̍t-gú|qid=Q1503147|lt=Monogatari}}'' about him.
== Name ==
The name Ame no Wakahiko means "a young boy in [[Takamagahara|heaven]]," and he is thought to be an exceptionally handsome youth.<ref name=":2" />
== Mythology ==
=== Sent to earth ===
In many versions, when [[Ame no Hohi]] did not send a word for three years, all the gods gathered up, and Ame no Wakahiko was one who was chosen to rule the earth. In many versions Amenowakahiko was given a bow.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Roberts |first=Jeremy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}}</ref>
In some versions, however, Ame no Wakahiko is the son of Ame no Hohi and Ame no Wakahiko was sent to earth to look for him.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&dq=Ame+no+Wakahiko&pg=PA6|isbn = 9781438128023|title = Japanese Mythology a to Z|year = 2009|publisher = Infobase}}</ref>
=== Death ===
In some versions, Ame no Wakahiko fell in love with {{ill|Shitateruhime|fr|Shitateruhime|ja|シタテルヒメ|simple|Shitateru-hime|zh|下照姬|qid=Q11307233}}. Eight years later, after not receiving no report back, the gods sent a bird named Nakime down to earth to check in on him. Following the advice of a wise woman, Ame no Wakahiko used his bow to shoot the bird.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Ashkenazi |first=Michael |title=Handbook of Japanese mythology |date=2008 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-533262-9 |series=Handbooks of world mythology |location=Oxford |pages=114}}</ref> The bird was killed but the arrow flew all the way to heaven.
[[Takamimusubi]] saw the arrow and threw it back at the earth where it hit Ame no Wakahiko while he was laying in bed, killing him.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAj_PQ8o40sC&q=Takamimusubi|title=The East|date=1992|publisher=East Publications, Incorporated|language=en}}</ref> Other versions state that [[Amaterasu]] was the one who shot the arrow back at him.<ref>{{cite book | last=Abe | first=C. | title=Impurity and Death: A Japanese Perspective | publisher=Universal Publishers | year=2003 | isbn=978-1-58112-195-7 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlZxh5OaZxoC&pg=PA38 | access-date=2020-09-29 | page=38}}</ref>
This myth is the origin of a Japanese saying about the returning arrow.<ref name=":3" /> It is likely also a mythicisation of attempts made by the [[:en:Yamato State|Yamato state]] to impose its authority over neighbouring states.<ref name=":3" />
=== Funeral ===
After Ame no Wakahiko's death, his parents built a hut (喪屋 moya) for their son. [[Ajisukitakahikone]] went down to pay his respect. However, due to Ajisukitakahikone looking similar to Ame no Wakahiko he was mistaken to be Ame no Wakahiko brought back to life. Ajisukitakahikone was offended by this and destroyed the hut and kicked it. The hut landed in the land of Mino and became a mountain called Moyama.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter-url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi:_Chronicles_of_Japan_from_the_Earliest_Times_to_A.D._697/Book_II|title = Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Volume 1| chapter=Book II }}</ref><ref name=":1" />
=== Other tales ===
Another story of Ame no Wakahiko appears in Japanese medieval literature of the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|qid=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} ([[Otogi-zōshi]]), in a narrative very similar to the [[:en:Aarne-Thompson-Uther Index|Aarne-Thompson-Uther]] tale type ATU 425, "{{ill|Animal as Bridegroom|cs|Hledání ztraceného manžela|fa|جانور همچون داماد|ml|മണവാളനായി മൃഗം|ta|மணமகனாக விலங்கு|tl|Hayop bilang Nobyo|uk|Тварина як наречений|qid=Q108179360|lt=The Search for the Lost Husband}}",<ref>김환희 [Hwan Hee Kim]. "<구렁덩덩신선비>와 「아메와카히코조시」의 친연성에 관한 비교문학적인 고찰" [A Comparative Study of the Affinities between the Korean Folktale of “the Serpent Husband” and the Japanese Story of “Ame no Wakahiko-zōshi”: a Study of <ATU 425 The Search for the Lost Husband> tales in Korea and Japan]. In: 민족문화연구 no. 63 (2014): 123. doi: 10.17948/kcs.2014..63.123</ref> or to the Graeco-Roman story of ''{{ill|Cupid and Psyche|ca|Cupido i Psique|de|Amor und Psyche|el|Έρως και Ψυχή (Μεταμορφώσεις)|fa|پسوخه و کوپیدو|it|Amore e Psiche|jv|Cupid lan Psyche|ko|큐피드와 프시케|lfn|Psice e Eros|lmo|Amor e Psiche|lt|Erotas ir Psichė|my|ကျူးပစ်နှင့် ဆိုက်ကီး|no|Cupid og Psyche|pnb|کیوپڈ تے سائیکی|pt|Amor e Psiquê|ro|Amor și Psyche|ru|Амур и Психея|sh|Kupidon i Psiha|simple|Cupid and Psyche|sl|Kupid in Psihe|sr|Ерос и Психа|th|คิวปิดและไซคี|tl|Kupido at Psique|uk|Амур і Психея|ur|کیوپڈ اور سائیکی|vi|Cupid và Psyche|zh|丘比特与普塞克|qid=Q135662|lt=Cupid and Psyche}}'', by writer {{ill|Apuleius|an|Apuleyo|anp|अपुलियस|ar|لوكيوس أبوليوس|arz|لوكيوس ابوليوس|ast|Apuleyo|az|Apuley|azb|آپولیوس|be|Апулей|be_x_old|Апулей|bg|Апулей|bn|লুসিয়াস এপুলিয়াস|ca|Luci Apuleu|co|Apuleiu|cs|Lucius Apuleius|da|Apulejus fra Madaura|de|Apuleius|el|Απουλήιος|eo|Apuleo|es|Apuleyo|et|Apuleius|eu|Apuleio|ext|Apuleyu|fa|آپولیوس|fi|Apuleius|fr|Apulée|frp|Apoulèyo|gl|Apuleio|ha|Apuleius|he|אפוליוס|hr|Apulej|hu|Lucius Apuleius|hy|Ապուլեոս|id|Apuleius|io|Apuleius|is|Apuleius|it|Apuleio|ja|アプレイウス|ka|აპულეიუსი|kab|Afulay|ko|아풀레이우스|ku|Apuleius|la|Lucius Apuleius|lfn|Apuleio|lt|Apulėjus|lv|Apūlijs|mk|Апулеј|ml|അപൂലിയസ്|mwl|Apuleio|nl|Lucius Apuleius Madaurensis|no|Lucius Apuleius Platonicus|oc|Apulèi|pl|Apulejusz (pisarz)|pt|Apuleio|ro|Apuleius|ru|Апулей|scn|Apuleiu|sh|Apulej|shi|Afulay|simple|Apuleius|sk|Lucius Apuleius|sl|Apulej|sq|Apulei|sr|Апулеј|sv|Apuleius|tg|Апулей|th|แอปยูลีอัส|tl|Apuleyo|tr|Apuleius|uk|Апулей|ur|اپولیوس|uz|Apuley|wuu|阿普列尤斯|zgh|ⴰⴼⵓⵍⴰⵢ|zh|阿普列尤斯|zh_min_nan|Apuleius|qid=Q170512|lt=Apuleius}}.<ref>{{ill|Noriko T. "Transforming an Ancient Myth into a Popular Medieval Tale". In: ''Japan on the Silk Road''. Leiden, The Netherlands: Brill, 2017. p. 339. doi: https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004274310_018</ref> while French curator {{ill|Jeannine Auboyer|af|Jeannine Auboyer|ar|جانين أوبوايه|arz|جانين اوبوايه|de|Jeannine Auboyer|fr|Jeannine Auboyer|qid=Q28377863|lt=Jeannine Auboyer}} dated the manuscript to ca. 1450.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Auboyer |first1=Jeannine |title=The Oriental world: India and South-East Asia |date=1967 |publication-place= New York |publisher= McGraw-Hill |isbn= |page=151 }}</ref>
In this tale, Prince Ame no Wakahiko takes the form of a serpent. One day, he delivers a letter to the maidservant of a wealthy man. The maidservant gives the letter to her master, who opens it: within, a command for the man to surrender his three daughters to the serpent in marriage, else it will kill his entire family. The man's two elder daughters refuse to marry the animal, but the youngest decides to be married to the snake.
The letter also instructed the man to build a palace near a pond, which is to serve as the couple's residence after their marriage. Soon, the human woman is delivered to the palace to await for her snake husband. An enormous serpent emerges from the pond and talks to its bride, assuaging her fears and asking for her to cut off his head. The human bride does as intended "with the blade of a fingernail clipper", and a handsome man comes out of the snakeskin. The man hides the snakeskin in a Chinese box and they enjoy their marital life. He later reveals he is a heavenly deity named Dragon Prince (or Dragon King - a ''kairyūō''),<ref>Reider, Noriko T. "A Demon in the Sky: The Tale of Ame no Wakahiko, a Japanese Medieval Story". In: ''Marvels & Tales'' 29, no. 2 (2015): 265. Accessed June 28, 2021. doi:10.13110/marvelstales.29.2.0265.</ref> and that he must travel somewhere, and asks her to wait for his return. He also begs his wife not to open the chest, lest she will never see him again. His wife asks him what can she do to find his way to him, and he answers that she must seek a woman in Kyoto and buy a gourd.
After some time, the wife is visited by her sisters, who discover that their brother-in-law, the snake, is in fact a handsome man. Spurred by envy, they convince their youngest sister to open the Chinese box.<ref>Nakawaki Hatsue. "Japanese Heroine Tales and the Significance of Storytelling in Contemporary Society". In: ''Re-Orienting the Fairy Tale: Contemporary Adaptations across Cultures''. Edited by Mayako Murai and Luciana Cardi. Detroit: Wayne State University Press. 2020. p. 152. {{ISBN|978-0-8143-4537-5}}.</ref> Only smoke comes out of the box, and later she learns he cannot return to her. She must, then, seek him out.
She goes to Kyoto, buys a gourd and uses its vines to reach the heavenly realm.<ref>Rumpf, Fritz. “Über Japanische Märchen Hagoromo (Das Federkleid)”. In: ''T’oung Pao'' 33, no. 3/4 (1937): 236-237, 249. http://www.jstor.org/stable/4527134.</ref> Now on Heaven, the girl asks directions from a man in hunting robes (the {{ill|Venus|en|Venus|qid=Q313|lt=Evening Star}}), then from a man with a broom (the Edited by Keller Kimbrough and Haruo Shirane. New York Chichester, West Sussex: Columbia University Press, 2018. pp. 169-170. {{ISBN|9780231184472}}. https://doi.org/10.7312/kimb18446-003</ref> At last, the girl enters the mansion and finds her heavenly husband, but he changes her into objects (an armrest, then a fan or a pillow) to hide her from his father, an ''{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|qid=Q730052|lt=Oni}}''. Eventually, the oni father-in-law discovers her and sets four tasks on his son's human wife: to herd a thousand cattle in one day and one night, to transport one million grains of rice from one granary to another, to stay in a warehouse full of centipedes, and in a warehouse full of snakes. She accomplishes all four tasks with her husband's assistance, since he gave her a magical sleeve. At the end of this tale, the oni father  lets his son and the wife meet once a month, but she mistakes it for "once a year" and thus, the lovers can only reunite during the ''{{ill|Tanabata|en|Tanabata|qid=Q1193996|lt=Tanabata}}''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Komatsu |first=Kazuhiko |title=[www.persee.fr/doc/ephe_0000-0002_2002_num_115_111_12068 Conférence de M. == Shrines of worship ==
{{expand section|date=September 2021}}
Ame no Wakahiko is enshrined at Abiko Shrine in {{ill|Aishō, Shiga|en|Aishō, Shiga|qid=Q1346806|lt=Aishō, Shiga}} and Iwakura Shrine in {{ill|Shinshiro|en|Shinshiro|qid=Q694923|lt=Shinshiro, Aichi}}.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=安孫子神社（滋賀県豊郷駅）のアクセス・お参りの情報 ｜ホトカミ|url=https://hotokami.jp/area/shiga/Hmstr/Hmstrtr/Dpzyp/80970/|access-date=2020-09-29|website=ホトカミ}}</ref>
